title: Largest box is o_p(log n) when m/n tends to zero
statement: Conjecture 18.4. If rho > 0 and m/n -> 0, then Y(1) = o_p(log n). [Context, same page: Theorem 18.3 gives, for 0 < lambda < nu, Y(1) <= log n / log(rho/tau) + o_p(log n); the source writes: 'We conjecture that Theorem 18.3 holds also for lambda = 0. Since then tau = 0, this means the following. (This seems almost obvious given the result for positive lambda in Theorem 18.3, where the constant 1/log(rho/tau) -> 0 as lambda -> 0 and thus tau -> 0, but there is no general monotonicity and we leave this as an open problem.)'] Notation of the source: w = (w_k) is a weight sequence, Phi(t) = sum w_k t^k has radius rho, Psi(t) = t Phi'(t)/Phi(t), nu = Psi(rho) (with nu = 0 when rho = 0), B_{m,n} is the random allocation of m balls in n boxes with weight prod w_{Y_i}, Y(1) >= Y(2) >= ... are the ordered box counts, m/n -> lambda, and for lambda < nu, tau in (0,rho) solves Psi(tau) = lambda and xi has the law pi_k = w_k tau^k/Phi(tau) (xi^(n) uses tau_n = tau(m/n)); the tree case is m = n-1.

attempt.method: Compare the two available routes: (a) monotonicity in m, which would sandwich m/n -> 0 below every fixed lambda and give the bound log n/log(rho/tau(lambda)) for every lambda > 0, hence o_p(log n); (b) the direct local estimate P(Y_1 = k) = w_k Z(m-k, n-1)/Z(m,n) from (18.14) with a union bound over the n boxes.
attempt.result: Route (a) is exactly what the source says is missing: for the multinomial weights w_k = 1/k! a ball-by-ball coupling shows Y(1) is stochastically nondecreasing in m, but for a general weight sequence there is no coupling of B_{m,n} and B_{m+1,n} that only moves one ball, because the conditional law of the extra ball's box depends on the whole configuration through w_{Y_i+1}/w_{Y_i}. Route (b) reduces the conjecture to a single estimate: with tau_n = tau(m/n) -> 0, the heuristic value is P(Y_1 >= k) ~ w_k tau_n^k/Phi(tau_n) for k of order log n, so n P(Y_1 >= k) -> 0 as soon as k >= k_n := (1+eps) log n / log(1/tau_n), and k_n = o(log n) precisely because tau_n -> 0. So the conjecture follows from: Z(m-k, n-1)/Z(m,n) <= C tau_n^k / Phi(tau_n) uniformly for k <= k_n when m/n -> 0.
attempt.obstruction: Lemma 13.1 of the source (the local limit theorem behind (18.14)) is proved for fixed lambda in (0, nu); when lambda_n = m/n -> 0 the laws of xi^(n) degenerate (mass at 0 tends to 1, variance tends to 0), and the Gaussian local limit theorem must be replaced by a Poisson-regime one in the range m << n and glued to the Gaussian regime when m is comparable to n. Nobody seems to have written that uniform statement; without it the union bound has no input.
attempt.key_identity: P(Y_1 = k) = w_k Z(m-k, n-1)/Z(m,n) (source (18.14)); the conjectured threshold k_n = log n/log(1/tau_n) = o(log n) because tau_n -> 0.

attempt.method: Identify what the proof of Theorem 18.7 needs from lambda > 0 and ask whether each input survives lambda_n -> 0: (1) the local limit theorem for sums of n-1 copies of xi^(n) at the point m-k (Lemma 13.1), (2) the comparison of Y_1 with xi^(n) via (18.14), (3) the Poisson approximation of the number of boxes above a level by dependency-graph or Chen-Stein arguments.
attempt.result: Inputs (2) and (3) are insensitive to lambda: (18.14) is an identity, and the Poisson approximation only uses that the events {Y_i >= h} are negatively dependent under the fixed-total constraint, which is a consequence of the product structure and holds for every m. Input (1) is the whole question: when m/n -> 0 the variance of xi^(n) tends to 0 and the local CLT is replaced by a local Poisson limit for the number of non-empty boxes. In the regime m = o(n) the natural statement is that S_{n-1} := sum of n-1 copies of xi^(n) satisfies P(S_{n-1} = m-k)/P(S_{n-1} = m) -> 1 uniformly for k = o(sqrt(m)) (a Poisson-type local ratio limit), and if that holds then (i)-(vi) go through verbatim with xi^(n).
attempt.obstruction: A local ratio limit theorem for triangular arrays whose step law tends to a point mass at 0, uniform over the two regimes m << n and m of order n, is not in the literature I know of; the standard Gnedenko-type local theorems assume a fixed step law or a fixed limiting variance. The problem is therefore a question in local limit theory rather than about trees.
attempt.key_identity: (18.14) P(Y_1 = k) = w_k Z(m-k, n-1)/Z(m,n); the missing input is the ratio Z(m-k,n-1)/Z(m,n) for lambda_n -> 0.

statement: Problem 18.10. Does d_TV(Y(j), xi_(j)) -> 0 hold for every fixed j, under the assumptions of Theorem 18.7? attempt.method: Reduce the total variation statement for Y(j) to a total variation statement for the point process of large boxes: both Y(j) and xi_(j) are functionals of the counting processes k -> N[k, infinity) and k -> N-bar[k, infinity), so d_TV(Y(j), xi_(j)) <= d_TV(law of (N[k,infinity))_{k >= h}, law of (N-bar[k,infinity))_{k >= h}) for any level h with N[h,infinity) >= j w.h.p.
attempt.result: With h = h(n) chosen so that n P(xi >= h(n)) -> alpha finite and large, both counting processes above h are Poisson-like point processes with O(1) points, and the total variation distance between the two restricted processes is controlled by (a) the Poisson approximation error for each, which the proof of (i) already bounds, and (b) the local error sup_k |P(Y_1 = k)/P(xi = k) - 1| over k >= h, which is what the proof of (vi) for j = 1 establishes through (18.14) and the local limit theorem. So the problem reduces to running the j = 1 argument on the joint local law of the top j boxes, i.e. a multivariate version of the local estimate: P(Y_1 = k_1, ..., Y_j = k_j) = prod w_{k_i} Z(m - sum k_i, n-j)/Z(m,n), and the same local limit theorem applies to Z(m - sum k_i, n - j) as long as sum k_i is in Lemma 13.1's range.
attempt.obstruction: The only place where care is needed is the range of k: when nP(xi >= h(n)) is bounded, the top boxes have sizes h(n) that can be of order sqrt(n) or larger for heavy-tailed xi (sigma^2 < infinity allows P(xi >= k) ~ k^{-2-eps}), and then the sum of j such values may leave the range of the local limit theorem used for j = 1. Whether the proof for j = 1 already handles k of order sqrt(n) is what has to be checked in the source; if it does, the multivariate version is the same argument. This is a verification, not a new idea, which is consistent with the source's own expectation.
attempt.key_identity: P(Y_1 = k_1, ..., Y_j = k_j) = prod_{i<=j} w_{k_i} Z(m - sum k_i, n-j)/Z(m,n).

attempt.method: Test the two implications against the classes where a local limit theorem for S_{n-1} is available at criticality with infinite variance: (a) xi in the domain of attraction of an alpha-stable law, 1 < alpha < 2, where the stable local limit theorem replaces Lemma 13.1; (b) the Cauchy case alpha = 1 (Kortchemski-Richier).
attempt.result: In class (a) the proof scheme of Theorem 18.7 survives: P(Y_1 = k) = w_k Z(m-k,n-1)/Z(m,n) and the stable local limit theorem gives Z(m-k,n-1)/Z(m,n) -> 1 uniformly for k = o(a_n) where a_n is the stable norming (order n^{1/alpha}), while for k of order a_n or larger the ratio is bounded by the stable density ratio, which is bounded above by a constant; hence n P(Y_1 >= h(n)) <= C n P(xi >= h(n)) -> 0 in (ii), and (iii) follows from the lower bound of the same ratio on {k <= a_n x} plus the second moment method. So (ii)-(iii) should hold in the stable domain; what is left is the Cauchy case and the case sigma^2 = infinity outside every domain of attraction. In the Cauchy case the answer to (ii) is decided by comparing the Kortchemski-Richier maximal degree scale with the level h(n) at which n P(xi >= h(n)) -> 0: if the maximal degree is of order n/ell(n) for a slowly varying ell while the level is n L(n) for the tail slowly varying function L, the comparison is a computation with the two slowly varying functions and I did not carry it out.
attempt.obstruction: Outside domains of attraction there is no local limit theorem for S_{n-1} at all, and (18.14) then gives nothing; a proof in that generality would need a local estimate for a sum of i.i.d. centered variables with infinite variance at a point of order n, which is genuinely open ground.
attempt.key_identity: (18.14) with the stable local limit theorem: Z(m-k,n-1)/Z(m,n) -> 1 uniformly for k = o(a_n) when xi is in a stable domain of attraction.

attempt.method: Ask what a weight sequence would have to look like for the excess (lambda - nu)n balls to prefer many boxes of size o(n) at EVERY n, and compare with the constraints rho > 0, Phi(rho) < infinity, rho Phi'(rho) < infinity that define 0 < nu < infinity. Write g(k) = log(w_k rho^k) and note that merging two large boxes of sizes a, b into one box of size a+b (leaving an empty box) multiplies the configuration weight by w_{a+b} w_0/(w_a w_b) = w_0 exp(g(a+b) - g(a) - g(b)).
attempt.result: A small rigidity lemma: g cannot be subadditive (g(a+b) <= g(a) + g(b) for all a, b), i.e. splitting cannot be weight-favoured at all scales simultaneously. Proof: if g is subadditive then by Fekete's lemma g(k)/k -> inf_k g(k)/k =: L in [-infinity, 0]; L < 0 would make w_k rho^k decay exponentially, so the radius of Phi would exceed rho, a contradiction; L = 0 forces g(k) >= 0, i.e. w_k rho^k >= 1 for all k, contradicting Phi(rho) < infinity. So every weight sequence with 0 < nu < infinity has infinitely many pairs (a,b) with g(a+b) > g(a) + g(b), i.e. scales at which merging is weight-favoured. This is consistent with the source's conjecture and explains why Examples 18.36-18.37 only achieve Y(1)/n -> 0 along subsequences: the sequences alternate scales where merging is favoured with scales where it is not. It does not prove the conjecture, because the entropy factor (which boxes carry the large counts, at most n per box) and the sizes actually realised at a given n are not controlled by the pairwise weight comparison alone.
attempt.obstruction: To turn the lemma into the conjectured statement one needs that the merging-favoured pairs (a,b) occur at every scale with a+b of order (lambda - nu) n, i.e. a density statement for the set {k : g(k) > max_{a+b=k}(g(a)+g(b))} rather than mere infinitude; Fekete's argument gives infinitude only. A weight sequence built to have g nearly subadditive on longer and longer intervals separated by short 'merging' intervals is the candidate counterexample to the weaker conjecture and I could not decide whether it stays consistent with rho Phi'(rho) < infinity.
attempt.key_identity: Merging weight ratio w_{a+b} w_0/(w_a w_b) = w_0 exp(g(a+b) - g(a) - g(b)) with g(k) = log(w_k rho^k); g subadditive is incompatible with rho being the radius of convergence and Phi(rho) < infinity.

attempt.method: Separate the two mechanisms in the source's example: (1) superexponential growth of w on its support, which favours putting balls together (for w_k = k!, w_a w_b = w_{a+b}/binom(a+b, a) <= w_{a+b}), and (2) gaps in the support, which forbid box sizes outside supp(w) and are the only reason Y(1) can be o(n) at some n. Then ask whether gaps can keep Y(1) = o(n) for ALL large n.
attempt.result: With s_1 < s_2 < ... the support points, a box can only hold s_j balls. If Y(1)/n -> 0 along the full sequence, then in particular at n = s_j + 1 (tree case m = s_j) the configuration with one box of size s_j and n-1 empty boxes, which has weight n w_{s_j} w_0^{n-1}, must be beaten by configurations of r >= 2 boxes with sizes in the support summing to s_j. For w_k = k! on its support, each such configuration has weight at most w_{s_j}/multinomial(s_j; a_1, ..., a_r) times w_0^{n-r}, and the number of such configurations is at most n^r/r!; the multinomial coefficient for r parts each at least 1 is at least s_j = n-1, so each extra box costs a factor of order 1/n against an entropy gain of order n: the comparison is at the same order and is decided by constants and the exact support, so the question is about the fine structure of supp(w), not about the growth rate. For weights growing faster than factorially the penalty beats the entropy n per box and the single box of size s_j wins at n = s_j + 1, so Y(1)/n -> 0 fails at those n; this suggests the answer NO for all sufficiently fast growing weights and leaves the factorial-rate boundary open.
attempt.obstruction: The comparison at n = s_j + 1 only shows Y(1) = s_j w.h.p. at those n when the penalty beats entropy; for weights growing at the factorial rate the two are of the same order and the outcome depends on the constants and on which sizes below s_j are in the support, so no general statement follows. attempt.method: Use monotonicity to get a pointwise bound on the weights and compare the weight cost of a second macroscopic box with the entropy gain of placing it. Monotone w with lambda > nu forces rho >= 1 (w bounded) and nu < infinity forces sum_k k w_k rho^k < infinity, hence sum_k k w_k < infinity; for a nonincreasing sequence, sum_{j <= k} j w_j >= w_k k^2/2, so w_k <= 2 (sum_j j w_j)/k^2 =: C/k^2 for every k. This pointwise bound is the key gain from monotonicity.
attempt.result: Heuristic answer YES, with the mechanism made explicit: a configuration with two boxes of sizes a, b >= eps n has weight at most w_a w_b <= C^2/(eps n)^4 in the two large boxes, while the competing configuration that keeps one box of size a+b-j and one of size j (any small j) has weight w_{a+b-j} w_j; a single deep drop of w cannot prevent this because the condensate may shed j balls to avoid it, and a nonincreasing w that is tiny on a whole interval [(1-eps)K, K] is tiny on [(1-eps)K, infinity), so the comparison is between w_{(1-eps)K-1} w_j (large) and w_a w_b with a, b < (1-eps)K, which is at most C^2/(a b)^2; the entropy gain of one extra macroscopic box is at most n, and n * n^{-2} -> 0. This gives (18.106) with (1-eps) in place of 1 for every eps > 0, i.e. (18.106)-(18.107), PROVIDED the non-condensed part behaves as in Lemma 18.31 and the number of macroscopic boxes is bounded, both of which Lemma 18.31 gives (the excess is (lambda - nu) n + o_p(n)).

attempt.method: Write r_i = w_{i+1}/w_i -> infinity. The weight change when b balls are moved from a box of size b into a box of size a >= b is w_{a+b} w_0/(w_a w_b) = w_0 prod_{i<b} (r_{a+i}/r_i). If r were eventually nondecreasing this product would be at least 1 beyond the monotone threshold and at least M^b with M -> infinity as a -> infinity, so merging any two boxes of macroscopic size would gain a factor exp(c n) against an entropy loss of at most n per box, and (18.106)-(18.107) would follow by a union bound. The question is what happens when r_i -> infinity without monotonicity.
attempt.result: Two observations. (1) The support is full (all w_k > 0), so the gap mechanism of Problem 18.40 is absent; any obstruction must come from oscillation of r. (2) Isolated spikes of r do not help splitting: if a spike sits at index i_0 < b, then instead of comparing (b, b) with (2b, 0) one compares with (2b-1, 1) or more generally (a+b-j, j), and the spike appears in both products for the right j, cancelling; what survives is the product of the non-spiky ratios, which is at least binom(a+b, b)-like and exponentially large. So a counterexample would need the ratios r_i to be smaller on [K/2, K) than on [j, K/2) in the sense of all partial products, for a whole range of j, which is in tension with r_i -> infinity as soon as the index sets are long. I therefore expect the answer YES, with a proof by a union bound over configurations with two boxes of size >= eps n using the merging identity with the shed-j trick (Lemma 18.31 is vacuous here since nu = 0: all lambda n balls are excess).
attempt.obstruction: The shed-j trick handles finitely many spikes but a rigorous statement needs a quantitative version: for a, b >= eps n there exists j <= eps' n with w_{a+b-j} w_j >= exp(c n) w_a w_b. attempt.method: Uniform integrability of l_k(T_n)^r is equivalent to sup_n E[l_k(T_n)^r; l_k(T_n) >= x] -> 0 as x -> infinity. Locate where the mass could escape: l_k(T_n) is large only if some vertex at depth < k has a large outdegree, and the number of vertices at depth < k is tight (local convergence to T-hat). So E[l_k(T_n)^r; l_k >= x] is comparable to sum_{d >= x} d^r P(some vertex at depth < k of T_n has outdegree d), and in the limit tree the corresponding quantity is E[xi-hat^r; xi-hat >= x] with xi-hat the size-biased law, finite because E xi-hat^r = E xi^{r+1} < infinity.
attempt.result: Two partial statements. (a) Any moment condition strictly stronger than E xi^{r+1} < infinity suffices: if E[xi^{r+1} phi(xi)] < infinity for some phi increasing to infinity, then the proof of uniform boundedness in [59] applied to the function x^r phi(x) in place of x^r (it only uses the moment through the size-biased law) gives sup_n E[l_k(T_n)^r phi(l_k(T_n))] < infinity, and de la Vallee-Poussin gives uniform integrability. So the conjecture is only about the exact threshold. (b) At the threshold the conjecture reduces to a ratio limit statement: P(a fixed vertex at depth j < k of T_n has outdegree d) <= C P(xi-hat = d) uniformly in n and in d <= n, because then E[l_k(T_n)^r; l_k >= x] <= C' E[xi-hat^r; xi-hat >= x/k] -> 0. For d = o(n) the ratio is P(xi = d) Z_{n-d}/Z_n times the spine correction, and Z_{n-d}/Z_n -> 1 uniformly for d = o(n) by the local limit theorem; the range d comparable to n has probability of order n P(xi = d), and the contribution sum_{d >= cn} d^r n P(xi = d) is at most n^{r+1} P(xi >= cn) -> 0 because E xi^{r+1} < infinity forces d^{r+1} P(xi >= d) -> 0.
attempt.obstruction: Part (b) is a sketch: the uniformity of the ratio P(deg = d)/P(xi-hat = d) over d up to order n requires a local limit theorem with a uniform error term over the full range of the conditioning, which the source's Lemma 13.1 provides only for d = o(n); assembling the ranges with the right constants is routine but not done here, and the non-integer r case needs the fractional-moment version of [59, Theorem 1.13], which is not available.
attempt.key_identity: E xi-hat^r = E xi^{r+1} for the size-biased law; escape of mass needs a vertex at depth < k with outdegree of order x.

attempt.method: Treat N_d as a function of the i.i.d. sequence xi_1, ..., xi_n conditioned on S_n = sum xi_i = n-1 (cyclic lemma). Unconditioned, N_d is Binomial(n, pi_d). The conditioning acts through the covariance of 1{xi = d} with xi: heuristically, conditioning on S_n = n-1 subtracts (S_n - (n-1)) Cov(1_{xi=d}, xi)/Var xi from N_d, which produces exactly Kolchin's variance correction -(d-1)^2 pi_d^2/sigma^2 (note Cov(1_{xi=d}, xi) = (d-1) pi_d for a critical law).
attempt.result: Prediction for the sigma^2 = infinity case: the correction coefficient Cov(1_{xi=d}, xi)/Var xi vanishes, so (N_d - n pi_d)/sqrt(n) should converge to N(0, pi_d(1-pi_d)), i.e. Kolchin's formula (20.6) with the last term dropped, and jointly in d with covariances pi_d delta_{dl} - pi_d pi_l, i.e. (20.7) without the last term. Reduction: this follows from a bivariate local limit theorem for (sum_i 1{xi_i = d}, S_n) with one Gaussian marginal at scale sqrt(n) and one stable (or merely infinite-variance) marginal at scale a_n >> sqrt(n): P(N_d = j | S_n = n-1) = P(N_d = j, S_n = n-1)/P(S_n = n-1), and conditionally on N_d = j the sum S_n is a sum of j copies of d and n-j copies of xi conditioned on xi != d, whose local limit at n-1 is insensitive to j - n pi_d = O(sqrt n) because that shifts the target by O(sqrt n) = o(a_n). So in the stable domain of attraction the answer to the second question should be YES with the modified variance, and the proof is a two-step local limit argument. For 0 <= nu < 1 (condensation) the same heuristic applies to the non-condensed part: the giant vertex changes N_d by at most one, so N_d - n pi_d should again be asymptotically N(0, pi_d(1-pi_d)) at least for power-law weights where Theorem 18.33 holds.

attempt.method: Reduce the height to fluctuation theory of the Lukasiewicz walk. With S_i = sum_{l <= i} (xi_l - 1), the depth of the vertex coded at time i equals the number of weak ascending ladder epochs of the reversed walk (S_i - S_{i-l})_{l <= i}, which has the same step law xi - 1 (a law bounded below by -1, centered, with infinite variance). By Sparre Andersen, the first weak ascending ladder epoch T satisfies 1 - E s^T = exp(-sum_{k>=1} s^k P(S_k >= 0)/k), so the number of ladder epochs up to time n is of order n P(T > n) and P(T > n) is governed by exp(-sum_{k <= n} P(S_k >= 0)/k).
attempt.result: Heuristic criterion: H(T_n)/sqrt(n) -> 0 iff sum_{k <= n} (P(S_k >= 0) - 1/2)/k -> -infinity. Sanity checks: for sigma^2 < infinity the summand is O(k^{-3/2}) (Berry-Esseen with the skewness term) so the sum converges and H is of order sqrt(n), matching (20.10); in the spectrally positive alpha-stable domain P(S_k >= 0) -> 1 - 1/alpha < 1/2, the sum is -(1/alpha - 1/2) log n and the criterion gives H of order n^{1 - 1/alpha}, matching Duquesne. So the conjecture reduces to the one-dimensional statement: for every centered law on {-1, 0, 1, ...} with infinite variance, sum_{k} (P(S_k >= 0) - 1/2)/k = -infinity. Since the steps are bounded below and have infinite variance, the walk is skewed to the right (rare large positive jumps, steady small negative steps), so P(S_k >= 0) < 1/2 for large k is the expected sign; the question is the rate.
attempt.obstruction: Two gaps. (1) The passage from typical depth (ladder-epoch count for one time i) to the maximum over i under the excursion conditioning is a constant-factor statement in the stable case but I do not have it in general; (2) the one-dimensional statement itself: outside domains of attraction P(S_k >= 0) can oscillate, and an infinite-variance law can have P(S_k >= 0) - 1/2 of either sign along subsequences (large jumps can also be arranged to make S_k >= 0 likely at chosen scales), so the divergence of the sum is not obvious and may even fail for a contrived law, which would make the conjecture false. A concrete test: take P(xi >= x) ~ 1/(x^2 log x) (variance infinite but barely) and estimate P(S_k >= 0) - 1/2 by a truncated Berry-Esseen expansion; I did not complete it.

attempt.method: Compare with Conjecture 20.5 through the two universal inequalities (H(T_n) + 1) W(T_n) >= n (the n vertices sit on at most H+1 levels of size at most W) and, in the other direction, H(T_n) W(T_n) = O(n log n) in probability (Donderwinkel-Khanfir 2025, arXiv 2501.00458, for simply generated trees with arbitrary weights).
attempt.result: Conjecture 20.6 follows from Conjecture 20.5: if H/sqrt(n) -> 0 then W >= n/(H+1) >> sqrt(n). Conversely, by the Donderwinkel-Khanfir bound, W/sqrt(n) -> infinity implies H = O(n log n/W) = o(sqrt(n) log n), so the two conjectures are equivalent up to a logarithmic factor, and any progress on the ladder-epoch criterion stated in the attempt on Conjecture 20.5 transfers here. Independently, in the condensed critical Cauchy case (Kortchemski-Richier 2019) a vertex of degree >> sqrt(n) exists, so W >> sqrt(n) there directly, since W >= max outdegree.
attempt.obstruction: Nothing beyond Conjecture 20.5: the reduction is exact in one direction and loses a logarithm in the other, and the case where H/sqrt(n) does not tend to 0 but W/sqrt(n) still tends to infinity is not excluded by the trivial inequality.
attempt.key_identity: (H+1) W >= n; H W = O(n log n) (Donderwinkel-Khanfir).

attempt.method: Decompose T_n at its vertices of outdegree larger than K_n (K_n -> infinity slowly). By Lemma 18.31 of the source these 'hubs' carry (1 - nu) n + o_p(n) of the n - 1 edges. The height is at most (number of hubs on the deepest root-to-leaf path) plus the heights of the hub-free pieces.
attempt.result: Two reductions. (1) If condensation (18.106)-(18.107) holds then there is one hub of macroscopic degree and all other outdegrees are o(n); if in addition the non-condensed part has the subcritical law (pi_k) with an exponential tail then the hub-free pieces are subcritical Galton-Watson trees conditioned to have size at most o(n), whose heights are O(log n), and H = O(log n) as in Kortchemski's case. (2) In general, a height H >= x sqrt(n) requires a nested chain of hubs or long hub-free paths; a chain of r hubs of degrees d_1, ..., d_r uses sum d_i <= n edges, so r >= x sqrt(n) hubs forces most of them to have degree <= sqrt(n)/x, i.e. the excess mass spread over >> sqrt(n) boxes of size << sqrt(n), which is the scenario of Problem 18.39 (many medium boxes); the alternative, long hub-free paths, is excluded when the pieces are subcritical trees with exponential tails. So a NO answer to Problem 20.7 would require an irregular weight sequence for which the excess balls sit in >> sqrt(n) boxes AND these boxes are nested along a path rather than spread out; the second condition costs an extra factor since nesting r hubs along one path has probability decaying in r.
attempt.obstruction: Neither the tail of the non-condensed part (the pieces need not be conditioned subcritical GW trees when w is irregular, and rho = 0 is possible) nor the nesting cost is controlled by anything in the source; the argument is a description of the only possible counterexample shape, not a proof.
attempt.key_identity: H <= (number of hubs on a root-to-leaf path) + (max height of a hub-free piece); sum of hub degrees <= n.

attempt.method: Use W(T_n) >= max outdegree = Y(1) (tree case of the allocation) and (H+1) W >= n.
attempt.result: (a) Whenever Y(1) >> sqrt(n), in particular whenever Y(1) >= eps n along the whole sequence (the source's conjecture in Problem 18.39 applied to nu < 1 = lambda), W/sqrt(n) -> infinity. (b) Unconditionally, W >= n/(H+1), so a positive answer to Problem 20.7 gives a positive answer here. (c) Also unconditionally: by Lemma 18.31, boxes with more than K_n balls hold (1-nu) n + o_p(n) balls; if W = O(sqrt n) then every outdegree is O(sqrt n) and the number of vertices with outdegree in (K_n, C sqrt n] is at least c sqrt(n); whether that is compatible with the weights is again Problem 18.39's scenario. So Problem 20.8 is implied by either Problem 20.7 or the conjecture in Problem 18.39, and is strictly weaker than both.
attempt.obstruction: Only the irregular subcritical weights of Examples 18.36-18.38 type could give a negative answer, and for those neither Y(1) nor H is controlled; the problem has no content beyond Problems 18.39 and 20.7 unless such an example is exhibited.

Addario-Berry, 'Most trees are short and fat' (PTRF 2019) proves that for ANY offspring distribution (critical, subcritical or supercritical) the height of the size-conditioned tree has sub-Gaussian upper tails at scale sqrt(n); every weight sequence with rho > 0 is equivalent to a probability weight sequence (source, Section 4), so (20.12) holds for all w with rho > 0. What remains is the case rho = 0 (superexponential weights), which is not equivalent to any offspring distribution and is not covered by that paper as far as its abstract states. Kept for that remainder only.

attempt.method: For rho = 0 there is no probability weight sequence equivalent to w, so the exponential tilting that drives Addario-Berry's proof is unavailable. Instead use the structure of rho = 0 trees: the weights grow superexponentially, so by the merging comparison of Problem 18.42 large outdegrees are favoured and the tree is a bounded number of hubs with small pieces, unless the support of w has gaps.
attempt.result: For full support and w_{k+1}/w_k -> infinity, a height H >= h costs h nested vertices of positive outdegree, and each such vertex could instead merge its subtree into the hub, gaining a superexponential factor; this gives P(H >= h) <= (C/n)^{h - C'} or better, far stronger than (20.12). For sparse supports (Examples 18.37-18.38) the maximal degree can be forced to n/2 or n/4 along subsequences, but the remaining mass still sits in a few large boxes and the height stays logarithmic at worst; a height of order sqrt(n) would need sqrt(n) nested hubs, each of size at most sqrt(n), against superexponential weights that favour a single box. So the answer should be YES also for rho = 0, by an argument on the number of hubs rather than by tilting.
attempt.obstruction: The rho = 0 case includes weights whose support is so sparse that a box of the wanted size does not exist at scale sqrt(n) but does at scale n/2 (Example 18.37), and there the tree is forced into a few boxes anyway; the difficult intermediate case is a support with gaps at every scale, where both the hub count and the entropy of placing hubs must be balanced, exactly as in Problem 18.40. I have not produced a bound uniform over all such supports.
attempt.key_identity: Rho > 0 weight sequences are equivalent to offspring distributions (source Section 4), so Addario-Berry 2019 covers them; rho = 0 is not.

attempt.method: Propose a general formula through the ladder-epoch representation of depths (attempt on Conjecture 20.5): with T the first weak ascending ladder epoch of the walk with steps xi - 1, the mean depth of a uniform vertex of the unconditioned forest up to time n is of order n P(T > n), and the excursion conditioning changes this by at most constants in every case where both sides are known.
attempt.result: Conjectural answer for the critical case: E H(T_n) is of order n P(T > n), where by Sparre Andersen P(T > n) is the coefficient of s^n in (1-s)^{-1} exp(-sum_k s^k P(S_k >= 0)/k); equivalently, with rho_n := (1/log n) sum_{k <= n} P(S_k >= 0)/k, E H(T_n) is n^{rho_n + o(1)} whenever rho_n converges (the number of ascending ladder epochs up to n grows like n^{rho} when P(S_k >= 0) -> rho). Checks: finite variance gives rho_n -> 1/2 and sqrt(n); the spectrally positive alpha-stable domain gives rho_n -> 1 - 1/alpha and n^{1-1/alpha}, which matches Duquesne. The width then follows from E W of order n/E H up to logarithms by the two universal inequalities. For nu < 1 the formula does not apply (the walk has negative drift and the conditioning is singular); there the answer for power-law weights is log n and n, and for irregular weights the height is governed by the hub structure of Problem 20.7.
attempt.obstruction: The formula is a conjecture supported by the two known regimes, not a theorem; proving it requires the comparison between the excursion-conditioned walk and the unconditioned one at the level of ladder epochs without a scaling limit, and outside domains of attraction rho_n need not converge, in which case the growth rate itself need not be a power of n, which is presumably the content of the questions posed by Addario-Berry, Donderwinkel and Kortchemski.
attempt.key_identity: E[number of weak ascending ladder epochs up to n] is of order n P(T > n); Sparre Andersen: 1 - E s^T = exp(-sum_k s^k P(S_k >= 0)/k).
